job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Fatima Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I catch the 7:50 train to a furniture maker's head office, where I'm a junior buyer in the procurement team. I studied business and I started in September. I order screws, fabric and packaging, compare supplier quotes and chase late deliveries. I use an AI assistant for most of the comparing and the emails, which is probably why my boss thinks I'm quick. I live in a shared house with two housemates, and most months I count to the last day before payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but overhyped. It already helps me compare quotes in ten minutes instead of an hour, and if it stays like that, fine. I'd tell my housemates that it's a decent tool, not magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm in a good place for a plateau. I do a bit more than the team expects because the tool lets me. But the money is tight: my loan payment, a rent increase coming in March, and the furniture business is slow. I could be bored for years and still be poor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the assistant and learn the supplier database properly. I'd ask for a stretch project, like negotiating a better price with our packaging supplier. If it saves money, I can ask for a raise. I'd also look for a cheaper room, since rent is the biggest piece.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. A little restless, because I want things to move faster than a plateau allows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a raise mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About 150 a month, which would let me pay down my loan faster and have a small buffer. Right now I have around ten days of costs saved. A raise would take me out of that all-or-nothing feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How likely is the raise, honestly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fifty-fifty. My manager, Chidi, is fair but the budget is tight, and the company froze two hires in the summer. But if I come with numbers, it's hard to say no.

say: AI is **useful but overhyped**: quote comparison takes ten minutes instead of an hour.
think: The **money is tight**: loan payment, a rent rise in March and a slow furniture business.
I could be **bored** for years and still be poor.
do: Ask for a **stretch project**, such as negotiating with our packaging supplier.
Take the savings to ask for a **raise**, and find a cheaper room.
feel: **Steady**, with some restlessness at how slowly things move.
S0.quote: I could be bored for years and still be poor.
fieldNote: Already uses AI **daily** and treats it as her edge at work.
Money pressure is the real driver, not **technology**.
Plans to turn savings into a **raise**, with realistic odds.

steps.text: Ask Chidi for a stretch project on packaging prices
Negotiate a better rate with the packaging supplier and log the savings
Find a cheaper room before the rent rise in March

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's already changing how buying works, and the smart thing is to be the person who runs it. I'd tell colleagues to try the tools before the company mandates something worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, quotes, price checks, reorder emails and supplier chasing are all things the assistant can do. If one buyer with AI does the work of three, I'm the junior of the three. But I'm also the one who knows how to use it, so I'm hoping to be the one who stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up automated reorder alerts for the top 20 products and show the savings to Chidi. I'd volunteer to train the older buyers, which makes me useful. I'd also start applying in the evening to supply-chain analyst roles at other firms, so there's a plan B. And I'd save 100 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, and a little jumpy. It feels like being in a race where the rules are changing as I run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the older buyers don't want to be trained?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some don't. Arvid, who has been buying fabric for twenty-five years, says he trusts his phone and his nose. I'd still try, because if he's cut, it's not my fault, but it would feel awful. People like him know suppliers by their first names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a point where you'd leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company freezes my pay and cuts the team, yes. I'd rather be at a firm that sees AI as a way to grow. I'm not loyal to a company that isn't loyal to me.

say: Buying is already changing, so be the person who **runs it**.
I'd tell colleagues to try the tools before the company mandates something **worse**.
think: Quotes, price checks and reorder emails are things the assistant already does, so the **junior role** is exposed.
I know the tools, so I hope to be the one who **stays**.
do: Set up **reorder alerts** for the top 20 products and show Chidi the savings.
Apply for **supply-chain analyst** roles in the evening as a plan B.
feel: **Excited and jumpy**, like a race where the rules change as I run.
S1.quote: I'm not loyal to a company that isn't loyal to me.
fieldNote: Treats AI fluency as **job security**, with a plan B ready.
Feels a pang for older buyer **Arvid**, who trusts his phone and his nose.
Mood is anxious because her **junior seat** is exposed even with skill.

steps.text: Set up automatic reorder alerts for the top 20 products
Offer to teach older buyers the AI assistant over lunch
Apply to three supply-chain analyst roles each month
Save 100 a month towards a six-week buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is a shock, and we need rules. Companies and governments are not ready. I'd put it online without being dramatic and say what I know: the tools are real and they're getting better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I have a year, not two. A junior buyer with a plain pass is early to go. The assistant I use today is a toy compared with that. I'd have thin savings and a loan. My edge, that I use AI daily, would be everyone's edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to turn the next year into cash and a skill: pick up freelance supplier-sourcing work for small brands in the evenings, and save everything I can. I'd start a course in electrical installation or plumbing, partly as a fallback, since robots come 3 years later and that gives me some air. I'd also ask my aunt Rukhsana whether I could use her spare room for six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dizzy. I've been the one who says 'learn the tools', and now I'm not sure that's enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the tools stop being your edge. What does that do to your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my plan can't be about skills alone. It's about having a cushion and something people still pay for. I'd have to be a bit of a hedge fund of my own: freelance, savings, a trade, family. I'd spread the risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your aunt fit in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's the only relative with space, and she's said so. I'd hate to ask, but I'd ask. Pride is a luxury I won't afford in that world.

say: Two years is a shock, and we need **rules**.
I'd say what I know: the tools are **real** and getting better.
think: I'd have a **year**, not two, and a junior buyer with a plain pass goes early.
My edge, using AI daily, would be **everyone's edge**.
do: Take on **freelance sourcing** for small brands and save every spare coin.
Start a **plumbing or electrical** course as a fallback, and ask my aunt about her room.
feel: **Dizzy**, since 'learn the tools' might not be enough any more.
S2.quote: Pride is a luxury I won't afford in that world.
fieldNote: The most AI-fluent centrist finds her **edge disappears** in two years.
Builds a spread of **fallbacks**: freelance, savings, a trade and family.
Accepts asking **family** for help, setting aside pride.

steps.text: Take freelance sourcing jobs for small brands on weekday evenings
Save every spare coin in a six-month buffer
Start an evening plumbing or electrical installation course
Ask my aunt Rukhsana for her spare room

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to adapt, and that we shouldn't waste it. I'd tell people to build a skill that goes with the machines, like managing them, checking their work and talking to suppliers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel pretty good. By 27 I could be a senior buyer or head of a small team, or I could have started a sourcing agency. The risk is the company shrinking the team before I get there. So I'd see the next two years as a window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd become the go-to person for AI-driven buying at my firm and negotiate a proper title. I'd put 150 a month into savings and clear my smallest debt. I'd also open a small sourcing side business with a friend who does design. And I'd study for a supply-chain qualification in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Optimistic, with nerves. It's the one where being quick pays off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the sourcing business sell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finding reliable factories and handling the paperwork for small brands that can't afford a buyer. I'd use the AI to compare thirty suppliers in an afternoon and take a fee. It only works if I'm honest and fast, which I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That a platform does it all by 2031 and cuts out the middle person. I'd have maybe three good years of income. I'd put the money away and not buy anything silly.

say: Five years is enough to adapt, so we shouldn't **waste it**.
Build a skill that goes with the machines, like **managing and checking** them.
think: By 27 I could be a **senior buyer** or run a small sourcing agency.
The risk is the company shrinking the team **before I get there**.
do: Become the **go-to AI buying person** and negotiate a proper title.
Start a small **sourcing business** and put 150 a month into savings.
feel: **Optimistic, with nerves**, since being quick pays off here.
S3.quote: I'd use the AI to compare thirty suppliers in an afternoon and take a fee.
fieldNote: Sees a **window** of about three good income years and plans to bank them.

steps.text: Take over AI-assisted buying for the fabric category and ask for a title
Start a sourcing side business with a designer friend
Put 150 a month into savings and clear the smallest debt
Study for a supply-chain qualification on weeknights

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is generous, and it'd be foolish not to use it. I'd say we should agree now on retraining and fair sharing of the gains, before it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel quite good. I'd be 32 with savings, a deposit and a business that did well, or a good role. My worry is the opposite of panic: I'd get comfortable and miss the moment. And that I'd have helped build tools that took away other people's jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first years clearing my loan and building experience at two firms. Then I'd go full-time on a small sourcing and supply analytics business and hire one or two people. I'd put money aside for retraining the staff I hired. I'd keep learning the new tools every few months so I'm never behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of excitement. It's the only one where I could imagine buying a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd worry about building tools that take away jobs. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older buyers at my firm, like Arvid. If I automate their work, they lose out. I'd like to think I'd help them move, but I know people his age don't want to be moved. It's the part of the job nobody puts on the CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you deal with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them early, give them a real choice and ask the company to pay for training. I'd rather be honest and unpopular than quiet and guilty.

say: Ten years is generous, and it'd be foolish **not to use it**.
We should agree on **retraining** and fair sharing of gains now.
think: At 32 I could have savings, a **deposit** and a good business or role.
My worry is getting **comfortable**, and helping build tools that take others' jobs.
do: Clear my loan and work at **two firms** before starting a small analytics business.
Set money aside to **retrain** any staff I hire.
feel: **Calm**, with a bit of excitement, and a flat within reach.
S4.quote: I'd rather be honest and unpopular than quiet and guilty.
fieldNote: **Ten years** and an early start make this the one scenario where her income looks secure.
Carries **guilt** about automating older colleagues' work, and plans honest warnings.
Calm because her work and money feel **secure** in this picture.

steps.text: Clear the student loan in three years
Start a sourcing and supply analytics business at 27
Learn every new buying tool within a few months of release
Set aside 5 percent of income to pay for staff retraining

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my advantage would vanish and I'd have almost no savings. What would help is a cushion for the first year, free retraining and housing that I can afford. If I can't pay rent, nothing else works.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not the typical person who wants to be left behind. I try things early. But even I couldn't keep up in a world that moves that quickly, and I think a lot of people would be hurt.

headlineQuote: Even I couldn't keep up in a world that moves that quickly, and I think a lot of people would be hurt.
portrait: Fatima is a **22-year-old** junior buyer at a furniture maker, in a shared house with a heavy loan.
She uses AI every day and treats it as her **edge**, though she's centrist and cautious about who gains.
She plans early in every scenario: raises, side sourcing work, analyst job applications.
She feels for older colleagues like Arvid, whose work she might automate.
Her mood runs from uneasy to **alarmed** in two years, then to calm with a decade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because AI fluency would stop being an edge and she'd have almost no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A **first-year cushion**, free retraining and affordable housing, because rent comes before anything else.
